title: Recursion and memoization
summary: Watch naive recursion repeat itself exponentially, then cache answers to make it linear.

steps.title: The same question, asked again and again
body: The Fibonacci numbers are `0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...`: each is the sum of the two before. The recursive definition is beautifully short:
int Fib(int n) => n < 2 ? n : Fib(n - 1) + Fib(n - 2);
But `Fib(5)` calls `Fib(4)` and `Fib(3)`; `Fib(4)` calls `Fib(3)` **again**, and so on. The call tree doubles at every level: roughly `O(2ⁿ)` calls. Watch `calls` climb in the trace.

steps.prompt: Same function, `Fib(10)`. What does it print?
steps.explain: Doubling `n` from 5 to 10 took the calls from 15 to 177. `Fib(50)` would need about 40 billion calls.
hints: calls(n) = 1 + calls(n - 1) + calls(n - 2), with calls(0) = calls(1) = 1.

steps.title: Memoization: remember answers
body: Each `Fib(k)` always returns the same thing, so compute it **once** and store it. Before doing any work, check the cache:
if (memo.TryGetValue(n, out var known)) return known;
Now each value from 2 to `n` is computed once: `O(n)` time for `O(n)` memory. Watch `memo` fill up and the repeated calls return instantly.

code: if (memo.TryGetValue(n, out var known)) return known;

steps.prompt: The memoized version, `Fib(10)`. What does it print?
code: if (memo.TryGetValue(n, out var known)) return known;
steps.explain: Each of `Fib(10)` down to `Fib(2)` is computed once and makes two calls: 9 × 2 = 18, plus the first call. Compare 177 without the memo.

options: When the same subproblems are solved many times
When each call has a different, never-repeated input
steps.explain: Merge sort is recursive but never repeats a subproblem, so a memo would only waste memory. Overlapping subproblems are the signal.

steps.prompt: Memoize the number of ways to climb `n` stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
code: if (memo.__2__(n, out var known)) return known;
steps.explain: There is exactly one way to climb 0 or 1 stairs. Otherwise the last move was a 1-step or a 2-step, so the ways add up.

steps.title: Fast Fibonacci
prompt: Write `long Fib(int n)` for `0 <= n <= 90` using memoization. `Fib(90)` is `2880067194370816120`; without a memo it would never finish.
Put the memo outside the function (a top-level `var memo = new Dictionary<int, long>();` above it) or use a `long[]`.
solution: if (memo.TryGetValue(n, out var known)) return known;
hints: Check the memo before recursing: `if (memo.TryGetValue(n, out var known)) return known;`.
Store as you return: `return memo[n] = Fib(n - 1) + Fib(n - 2);`.

steps.title: Paths through a grid
prompt: A robot starts in the top-left cell of a `rows × cols` grid and may only move **right** or **down**. Write `long GridPaths(int rows, int cols)`: how many different routes reach the bottom-right cell.

Recursive idea: the last move into a cell came from above or from the left, so `paths(r, c) = paths(r - 1, c) + paths(r, c - 1)`, and a single row or column has 1 path. The tests ask for `GridPaths(30, 30)`; memoize on `(r, c)`, for example with a `Dictionary<(int, int), long>` or a `long[,]` inside the function.
solution: var memo = new Dictionary<(int, int), long>();
if (memo.TryGetValue((r, c), out var known)) return known;
return memo[(r, c)] = Paths(r - 1, c) + Paths(r, c - 1);
hints: Base case: when `r == 1` or `c == 1` there is exactly one path.
Write a recursive local function `Paths(r, c)` that checks and fills a memo keyed by `(r, c)`.
